summary: Describes how to extend sequence numbers at the endpoints of sliding window protocols without sending extra bits in the packet header. Finite sequence numbers wrap around and get reused, and the extended numbers help encryption and authentication algorithms avoid repeating input patterns. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a counter runs out and starts over, each side keeps a secret extra count so numbers never really repeat.

questions: how to prevent repeating sequence numbers
sequence number extension for tcp authentication
subtitle: Extend sequence numbers at endpoints to prevent wraparound without adding packet header bits.

tldr.problem: Sliding window protocols like TCP use finite sequence numbers that wrap around and repeat over long connections, which can cause problems for encryption and authentication algorithms that assume unique input values.
tldr.mechanism: Both endpoints maintain a local counter (SNE) that tracks how many times the sequence number field has wrapped around. By combining the SNE with the received sequence number, endpoints can reconstruct a larger sequence number space without transmitting extra bits in the protocol header.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints can use extended sequence numbers for encryption and authentication without modifying the protocol message format or adding header overhead, ensuring input bit patterns never repeat over the lifetime of a connection.

today: RFC 9187 is an Informational specification from January 2022 that formalizes the Sequence Number Extension technique with complete implementations and test vectors. SNE continues to be useful in protocol design for encryption and authentication, especially in long-lived connections.

sections.title: Extending Sequence Numbers Invisibly
sections.content:
Network protocols like TCP use sequence numbers to maintain message order and detect loss, but these numbers are represented in a fixed-size field (e.g., 32 bits) that eventually wraps around to zero and repeats. This wrapping can cause problems: encryption algorithms and authentication schemes like TCP-AO (TCP Authentication Option) require unique input values to avoid creating identical ciphertext or authentication codes for different messages.

This memo describes Sequence Number Extension (SNE), a technique introduced in RFC 5925 but formalized here with complete pseudocode and test cases. SNE allows endpoints to extend the sequence number space at the application layer without modifying protocol messages or adding header overhead. Both endpoints independently track and reconstruct extended sequence numbers based solely on the sequence numbers they receive.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocol messages have a sequence number in a limited space, like 0-255, which repeats forever. But for security, you want unique numbers that never repeat. SNE lets each side keep a secret count of how many times the numbers have wrapped, without anyone else needing to know about it.

sections.title: How Sequence Numbers Work
sections.content:
A sequence space is an unsigned integer with a fixed bit width (N bits), ranging from 0 to 2^N - 1. The transmitter increments these values by some increment K (where K is less than half the space, or 2^(N-1)). The receiver uses comparison to determine order: does X come before Y?

The key constraint is that receivers never jump backward or forward by more than half the sequence space (2^(N-1) - 1). This is typical in sliding window protocols where reordering is limited. For example, in a 32-bit sequence space, the distance between consecutive values should never exceed about 2 billion.

When a sequence number wraps (reaches the maximum and starts over), a receiver cannot tell if an incoming number is from before or after the wrap without additional information. An SNE counter solves this by tracking how many times the wrap has occurred.
sections.plainLanguage: A sequence number goes 0, 1, 2, ..., 255, then back to 0. The receiver knows the number came after 255 (not before) because numbers don't jump backward more than halfway across the space. SNE just counts how many times it has looped.

sections.title: Computing Extended Sequence Numbers
sections.content:
The transmitter can compute SNE trivially by incrementing a local counter every time the sequence number field wraps, or by keeping a larger local sequence number where the low bits are the message sequence number and high bits represent SNE. The transmitter typically does not send this information.

The receiver computes SNE from the received sequence number using the compute_sne() function, which maintains persistent state: the largest SNE and sequence number combination seen so far. When a message arrives, the function compares the new sequence number to the previous one: if they are close (within half the space), they are in the same SNE range; if they are far apart, the new value is in a different SNE range and SNE must be incremented or decremented.

This computation works correctly for any series of sequence numbers, as long as the series never jumps more than half the space backward from the largest value seen forward. This constraint is enforced by the protocol design itself and verified through the validator implementation and test suite.
sections.plainLanguage: When you get a new sequence number, you check: is it close to the last one? If yes, it is in the same wrap-around cycle. If no, then it wrapped. Update your secret count and use both together.

sections.title: Implementation and Validation
sections.content:
The memo provides complete C code for the compute_sne() function suitable for production use, plus a test harness. Protocol designers can verify their implementations against a validation suite containing 30 test cases that exercise both forward and backward jumps in sequence numbers, ensuring the implementation correctly handles wraparound in all scenarios.

Because SNE is computed locally from publicly visible sequence numbers, both endpoints automatically stay in sync without any protocol messages dedicated to SNE synchronization. The only requirement is that sequence numbers themselves are exchanged reliably and in order (or with reordering within the half-space limit).

SNE is not needed if messages are already unique through other means, such as timestamps or if the sequence number field is large enough never to wrap during the protocol's lifetime. For protocols like TCP-AO, where authentication codes must be unique to prevent replay, SNE is essential.
sections.plainLanguage: There is working code in the memo you can copy and adapt. The test cases show that it works for all the tricky situations with wrapped numbers. Both sides compute SNE the same way and stay in sync automatically.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
SNE should not be considered as adding entropy for encryption or authentication purposes. Because the extension is derived entirely from the sequence numbers already visible in messages, it does not provide additional randomness or protection. Its role is to ensure uniqueness, not to add secrecy.

However, this uniqueness property is critical for many security applications. Encryption algorithms and authentication codes require non-repeating input values to avoid generating identical ciphertexts or authentication tags for different messages. SNE enables this guarantee at the endpoints without protocol overhead.

The security of SNE-based schemes depends entirely on the security of the underlying encryption or authentication algorithm and on the protocol's ability to ensure that sequence numbers advance as assumed. Any violation of the reordering constraints (jumps of more than half the space) will cause SNE computation to fail.
sections.plainLanguage: The SNE itself is not secret; it is just math on public numbers. But it makes sure that when you encrypt or sign a message, you never use the same number twice, which is crucial for security.
